1001 AI, an artificial intelligence (AI) company based out of the GCC and UK, has secured US$30 million in a Series A funding round led by New York-based venture capital (VC) firm Lux Capital, as it looks to accelerate the deployment of its AI platform for critical infrastructure across the Gulf.  

Founded in 2025 by Jordanian entrepreneur Bilal Abu-Ghazaleh, 1001 develops AI systems that create a live digital model of critical infrastructure assets, operational processes, dependencies, and constraints. With its technology designed for deployment across aviation, ports and logistics, energy, manufacturing, and other industrial operations, 1001 aims to help operators anticipate disruptions, improve decision-making, and recommend or execute responses across complex physical systems, while enabling customers to build, own, and govern the technology locally.  

In an interview with Inc. Arabia, Abu-Ghazaleh shared that 1001 came into being thanks to his belief that the next industrial leap will come from AI that changes how the physical world actually runs. He also shared that choosing to build 1001 in the Middle East—home to some of the world's most critical infrastructure—was a deliberate decision.  

“For years, our region was treated as a source of capital,” Abu-Ghazaleh explained. “A place that funds technology rather than builds it. I think that era is over. The shift now is from capital to capability. From writing the check to owning the technology. The systems that run our most critical infrastructure should not be rented from abroad. They should be built, owned, and governed here. So, our mission is simple. We are building the AI operating system for critical infrastructure. The decision layer for the institutions that move the physical world. And we are building it here, in the region, for the region.”

The GCC sits at the center of global energy, logistics, aviation, finance, and trade. That creates an extraordinary opportunity not just to consume AI, but to build trusted AI systems for some of the world’s most complex, high-consequence operating environments.

I believe the Arab world has a once-in-a-generation opportunity to help define the AI era—not just invest in or participate in it. And there is no one better suited to turn that vision into reality than Bilal Abu-Ghazaleh and 1001 AI.

content:
A contractor told me he likes his estimators tracing and coloring rooms by hand.

Not because it is efficient. Because by the time they finish, they know the building.

His point was that the more automation his people use, the less familiar they are with the job.

That is a real cost, and I do not think it gets talked about enough.

Speed and familiarity are not the same thing.

A takeoff is not only how quantities get produced. It is also one of the ways a junior estimator learns what a building is.

What I would say is that not all of that learning comes from the counting itself.

Understanding scope, spotting what is missing, knowing where the risk sits in the drawings, that is the knowledge you want them building.

Tracing 400 rooms is repetition. But I would not dismiss his concern.

If you give a junior estimator a tool that gets them to the answer faster, you have to be deliberate about where they build judgment instead.

Curious whether anyone has thought about this for their own team.

We talk a lot about company culture in startups, but product culture is just as important but often overlooked.

Every great product company has one.

Apple’s product culture is simplicity and beauty.

Meta’s product culture is experimentation and speed. 

Product culture tells users what your company stand for. Internally, it sets the bar for how builders operate, especially PMs, designers, and engineers.

Not just what they build, but how they build it.

Be fast, but write quality code.
Move quickly, but think deeply.
Make it beautiful, but keep it simple.

These ideas often conflict.

That’s why defining your product culture early is crucial. 

It’s how trust and loyalty is built with your customers, and It becomes the compass for making decisions when your team encounters inevitable tradeoffs.

content:
One of the advantages construction gives us in building autonomous systems is speed. Or more precisely, the lack of it. 

An excavator's top speed is about 3 miles per hour. On a highway, a self-driving car moving at 65 mph needs to see hundreds of meters ahead to make safe decisions. Our machines don't need anything close to that range, which means the sensor technology available today already exceeds what we require. That margin translates directly into safety.

People often ask why we started with excavators. 

Excavators typically make up 20 to 25 percent of the equipment a general contractor operates. They're also one of the hardest machines to learn. An excavator has up to eight axes of motion: the boom, the stick, the bucket, a cab that rotates 360 degrees, and independent tracks. Controlling all of that simultaneously while reading the terrain takes years of practice. Most operators need at least five years to become truly skilled. 

That combination is what makes the excavator the right place to start. It's high volume, high complexity, and high demand. If we can build autonomy that works here, it opens the door to bulldozers, loaders, and every other machine on a job site. 

It's also where the labor gap is especially visible. Skilled heavy equipment operators are some of the hardest roles for contractors to fill, and excavation is critical path on nearly every project. If it falls behind, everything else falls behind with it. 

Excavators are where we start. Autonomous heavy equipment across construction, mining, and beyond is where we're headed.

content:
This year’s BuiltWorlds Robotics Top 50 List offers a revealing look at where construction robotics is gaining real traction—and what the next phase of automation may look like.

Across the Automated Machinery & Related Solutions category, the biggest theme is clear: robotics is moving beyond isolated demonstrations and into the workflows where labor constraints, safety risks, and repetitive work create the greatest opportunities.

In 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐡𝐦𝐨𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 & 𝐄𝐱𝐜𝐚𝐯𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠, autonomy is increasingly being delivered through retrofits, remote operation, and machine-control systems rather than requiring contractors to replace their fleets. That points to a market focused not just on technical capability, but on making automation practical for the equipment already operating on jobsites. 

Congratulations to Caterpillar Inc. Command, Gravis Robotics, Built Robotics, Teleo, HIVE, Komatsu Intelligent Machine Control, Xpanner, Pronto, and Bedrock Robotics!

𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 shows another compelling path forward. Remote-controlled and robotic systems are taking on hazardous, physically demanding work while allowing operators to work from a safer distance. Meanwhile, specialized approaches such as hydrodemolition demonstrate that robotics can improve not only productivity, but also the quality and precision of the work itself. Congrats to the teams at Conjet Group and BROKK!

And in 𝐌𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭, a new category of opportunity is emerging. Autonomous haulers, mobile robots, robotic hoists, and AI-enabled logistics platforms are targeting one of construction’s most persistent inefficiencies: moving people and materials around the jobsite.

A final congratulations to Daedong Robotics, FloMobility, KEWAZO, GoLe Robotics, and Cyphra!

Taken together, this year’s honorees suggest that construction robotics is becoming less about the robot itself and more about reimagining how work gets organized around increasingly autonomous equipment. The winners may ultimately be the technologies that fit seamlessly into existing workflows—not the ones that simply look the most futuristic.

As these technologies move from pilot projects into everyday construction workflows, where will contractors see the biggest opportunity to put robotics to work next? Let us know your thoughts in the comments 👇

content:
11 years ago, I started my company on an unemployment check.

I'd applied late. I told the man at the government office I'd lost my job, that I was sleeping at the hacker dojo, and I needed the $1,900 to buy some cameras that I would start an AI company with. I pitched him the idea for what eventually became Doxel AI — told him this would create lots of jobs one day if he let me in. I must've looked desperate, because he helped me out. 

I remember he said "Make us proud."

I didn't know anyone in construction or any investors. I was 24 and hadn't even held a job for more than six months. But I had a laptop. So I cold-emailed builders and stopped by their offices unannounced until one took a bet on me and wrote me a $120K PO for a pilot. 

I was terrified of the pilot going well — I didn't have enough money to scale the product if it did.

I went to my college professor for advice. He laughed, wrote me a check, and introduced me to Andreessen Horowitz. They didn't care that I had almost no work experience. They liked the idea and led our seed so we could go build it out.

Strangers helped in ways I didn't expect. A man sold me his Camry for $2,200 — heavily discounted — when he heard I was starting a company. An Uber driver in Kansas City overheard me talking about a deal we needed to win, ran out of the car as I stepped out at the airport, and said he'd pray for my company's success. A flight attendant once got a message to our lawyers mid-flight — through the cockpit — when the wifi died during a negotiation for a critical deal. 

Insanely talented people decided I wasn't entirely crazy and took a bet on building this company with me.

We have a long way to go. But off that $1,900 unemployment check and the bets of so many people along the way, today Doxel tracks construction for 4 of the 5 largest hyperscalers, 14 of the top 20 data center developers, 18 of the top 30 general contractors, 3 of the world's largest EV and battery makers, 2 of the world's top 5 pharma companies and 5 of the country's leading health systems.

Only in America.

Happy Independence Day!

In partnership with Sundt Construction, Champion Site Prep, Inc., and Zachry Construction Corporation, Bedrock-equipped machines are performing earthwork across three large-scale projects in Texas and Nevada.

This matters because America’s ability to reindustrialize depends on its ability to build: factories, energy facilities, water systems, data centers, new housing, and the roads that connect it all.

But the nation’s construction capacity has become a primary strategic bottleneck.

Major projects routinely face substantial schedule and cost overruns, and the persistent labor gap is still widening. The physical backbone of the American economy depends on an industry that is being asked to do more with less. Autonomous systems offer a path to expand our building capacity by multiplying the impact of every crew.

We’re giving contractors and their teams new tools to build more of what America needs, with greater safety, speed, and predictability. We started with excavators, but Bedrock’s mission extends far beyond a single machine type. It's about creating a new layer of autonomous orchestration for the equipment that shapes our world.

I’m so grateful to the many team members that have brought their unique expertise to this mission and to our close partners that have shown the trust in us to build this future together.

We’re so excited about the adventure ahead!

The world's cities share a common challenge—𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼 𝘄𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗴𝗼𝗼𝗱𝘀 𝘀𝗮𝗳𝗲𝗹𝘆, 𝘀𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗯𝗹𝘆, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗲𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗹𝘆? Solving this requires more than infrastructure alone; it demands a strong digital foundation that enables data-driven, AI-powered decision-making.

As part of the 𝗠𝗜𝗻𝗧 𝗠𝗼𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗦𝘂𝗺𝗺𝗶𝘁 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲, held from 𝟲–𝟴 𝗝𝘂𝗹𝘆 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲 at Indian Institute of Technology, Madras, we invited our distinguished speakers and collaborators to share their reflections on the ideas, partnerships, and innovations shaping the future of mobility.

🎙️ In this video, 𝗗𝗿. Ajay Gummalla, 𝗩𝗣 & 𝗖𝗼-𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿, Bedrock Robotics, 𝗙𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗳 The MInT Collaborative, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗕𝗼𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗳 The MInT Collaborative, shares his vision for building the digital infrastructure needed to power the next generation of intelligent cities.

Dr. Ajay Gummalla highlights that while every city faces the challenge of moving people and goods efficiently, 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗮'𝘀 𝗵𝗶𝗴𝗵-𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝘂𝗿𝗯𝗮𝗻 𝗲𝗻𝘃𝗶𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗲 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘅. One of the biggest barriers to solving mobility holistically is the lack of 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗶𝗴𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 that is robust enough for modern AI systems to understand and reason across the entire urban ecosystem.

At The MInT Collaborative, 𝗜𝗜𝗧 𝗠𝗮𝗱𝗿𝗮𝘀, we are working to bridge this gap by building the 𝗱𝗶𝗴𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗳𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲-𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘆 𝗰𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀. Through close collaboration with 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗿𝘀, 𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰𝘆𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗿𝘀, 𝗶𝗻𝗱𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘆 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗴𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁, we are developing scalable solutions that can transform urban mobility.

The future of mobility will be built on 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗶𝗴𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲, 𝘁𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗔𝗜, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗼𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻—creating intelligent urban systems that are scalable, resilient, and designed to address real-world challenges.

The recognition comes from BuiltWorlds' Equipment & Robotics Benchmarking survey, which draws on feedback from contractors working in the field every day. Being named alongside them reflects the trust our partners have placed in us as we work together to develop and validate autonomous systems for heavy equipment. 

Bedrock's mission is to multiply what skilled operators and crews can do on a job site, not diminish their role in it. This nomination is an early signal that the industry sees the same potential we do. 

Thank you to our partners who made this possible, and to the broader team building toward what's next.
